title: 8  The Kick-off
text:
8.1 A rough map of how we’ll work
Leon had spent the last few weeks preparing for this meeting. The agreement with Claire is in place, the team had been assembled, and the first appointments were scheduled. He had read about Spec-Driven Development, explored Event Modeling, and spent enough time in prooph board to feel comfortable showing other people around.
The meeting room is ready. Four chairs, a large whiteboard, coffee, and a short presentation. Leon deliberately kept the slides to a minimum. He doesn’t want to spend the first hour explaining a new methodology. They are here to build something, not to attend a seminar.
The first slide shows the project name.
Shelter Flow.
Leon looks around the table. The team is a mix of people who are eager to try something new and people who want to know whether the new thing is actually going to work. Everyone seems happy to leave the familiar routine of ERP development behind for a while.
He takes a breath.
He explains the agreement with Claire. They have three months, and everyone contributes half of their time. At the end of that period, they will sit together, look at what they have built and learned, and decide whether continuing makes sense.
He pauses to let that sink in. He doesn’t want anyone to think they are expected to defend a predetermined decision. The experiment is agreed upon. How they conduct it is still open.
Leon draws on the whiteboard. Four words appear in a circle, connected by arrows:
Storm → Design → Validate → Build
He gestures toward the four words.
The iteration looks neat on the screen. Four words, four steps, arrows pointing in one direction. Leon knows that real work rarely follows such a tidy path, but the sequence gives them somewhere to start.
Chris leans forward. The possibility clearly appeals to him.
Leon likes the idea. He also knows that none of them has evidence that it will work in their environment. He doesn’t want their enthusiasm to turn into expectations they cannot meet.
Mina has been listening quietly. She looks at the four words on the whiteboard.

title: 8  The Kick-off
text:
“I’ve been looking into Spec-Driven Development, and one approach that interests me is Event Modeling. The idea is to collaborate on understanding the business and then use that understanding to shape the software we build. Instead of starting with a pile of tickets, we work together on a model of what the system is supposed to do.”





“Storm means we explore the domain together. Design is where we work out what the software should do. Validate means we check whether our ideas make sense. And Build is where we turn them into working software.”





“And the agents build directly from the model?”





“That’s the idea. We want the model to become the specification the agents work from. They should get the context they need there, rather than receiving a ticket and having to guess what the rest of the system is supposed to do.”




“That could be really interesting. The agents already write a lot of code. If we can give them better context, maybe they can do much more than just implement individual tickets.”




“Exactly. But we need to find out how much context is enough, and how we make sure the model actually contains what the agents need.”

title: 8  The Kick-off
section: 8.2 The questions nobody can answer yet
text:
8.2 The questions nobody can answer yet


“What does Validate mean in practice? How do we know that the software the agents build behaves the way we intend?”


It is a fair question. Describing the intended behavior and verifying the implemented behavior are two different problems.


“That’s one of the things we need to work out. We have to find a way to validate what we model and check that the software does what we expect. I don’t have a complete answer yet.”


Mina nods. She isn’t looking for a polished answer. She wants to know whether the team takes the problem seriously. So far, at least, Leon doesn’t pretend to know more than he does.
Kim glances at the whiteboard again.


“Does this include user journeys and interaction design? And how?”


For Kim, that is where the product becomes real. She can imagine a model of business events, but she can’t yet see how it captures the journey a person takes through an application, the decisions they make, or the small details that make an interaction feel natural.


“As far as I understand, yes. But we need to discover together how it works and adjust it to our needs.”


Kim accepts the answer. She trusts Leon’s product judgment, and she is here because she cares about the project. Still, the question remains in the back of her mind. She wants to see how a model that everyone works on can express the details she normally captures in user journeys, designs, and product requirements documents.
Leon moves on. He doesn’t want to turn the first meeting into a debate about artifacts before they have even tried working together.


“I also hope we can avoid translating everything into separate documents before development starts. Ideally, the model gives us a shared place to work out what we mean and provides the agents with the specification they need. But I don’t know how far we can take that. We may discover that we still need other artifacts, or that we need to change how we work.”


He has spent a fair amount of time connecting these ideas in his own head. Now he has to make them useful to people who bring their own responsibilities, habits, and expectations to the project.
And the questions are reasonable. A model that looks convincing to its creator may still leave a designer wondering where the user journey belongs, a developer wondering how to validate the result, and an agent without the information it needs to implement the behavior correctly.
Leon closes the presentation.


“We don’t need to solve all of that today. We need to start working together and see what we discover.”


He opens prooph board and brings up a small model he prepared earlier. A photograph of a dog fills part of the screen.

title: 8  The Kick-off
text:
8.3 Meeting Caramelo


“This is Caramelo. His story is what got me thinking about the project in the first place.”


Leon heard the story from a shelter volunteer. A few weeks ago, while familiarizing himself with prooph board, he sketched its episodes in the tool. The result is not a complete Event Model, and he doesn’t present it as one. It is simply a story that helps them begin to understand the world they are entering.
The episodes touch on things like medical treatment, foster families, and adoption applications. They give the team a few concrete concepts to think about before meeting the people who actually work in a shelter.


“I’d like everyone to read the story before our workshop. Don’t worry about understanding everything yet. It’s there to give us a starting point and some context.”


Chris studies the screen.


“So we get to build something for a good cause, try new technology, and experiment with a different way of working. Sounds pretty good to me.”




“That’s the plan. Though I suspect the difficult part won’t be getting the technology to do something. It’ll be figuring out what we actually want it to do.”


Chris smiles. He doesn’t seem particularly worried about that possibility. For now, the prospect of working with AI agents on a new product is enough to make the project feel different from his regular work.
Leon also tells them that he has contacted Alex, the creator of prooph board. Alex has offered to help if they run into questions and, provided Shelter Flow is open source, to give them additional seats for free.


“Free tools and new technology. We’re off to a good start.”




“Let’s see if we can make good use of them first.”


There is still one important part of the preparation to discuss: the first workshop.

title: 8  The Kick-off
text:
8.4 Preparing for the first workshop
Leon has arranged a full day with Sarah Thompson, the director of the animal shelter. The entire team will participate. They need to understand the work from the people who do it, rather than design a system based on their own assumptions about how a shelter operates.
They are going to try Event Storming, something none of them has used before.


“The basic idea is pretty simple. We get everyone together in front of a wall and write down important things that happen in the business. We write them as events, in the past tense, on sticky notes. Everyone contributes, rather than having one person conduct an interview and take all the notes.”


He has read enough to understand the basic idea. He hasn’t yet experienced what happens when people with different perspectives try to agree on what actually happens in a business.


“We’ll start with Animal Intake. We don’t need to understand the whole shelter in one day. First, we need to understand what happens when an animal arrives and what the people involved need to do.”


Kim looks at the Caramelo story still open on the screen.


“I suppose we’ll find questions we don’t even know to ask yet.”




“I hope so.”


The meeting is nearly over. The team has a project, a rough plan, and a few ideas about how they might work. They also have several questions that nobody can answer yet.
For Leon, that is enough to begin.
Before they meet Sarah, everyone has one small task: read Caramelo’s story. The workshop will start with the work of a real shelter, not with a model the team has already decided is correct.
The experiment is underway.

title: 9  Discovering the Big Picture
text:
9.1 Getting started
The team is ready for its first Event Storming workshop. They’ve read a little about the method (Brandolini 2021) and spent some time with Caramelo’s story to familiarize themselves with the animal shelter domain. They know they’ll meet Sarah Thompson, the shelter director, and that she’ll help them understand how things work in the shelter.
But reading about Event Storming and actually doing it are two different things.
Leon takes responsibility for facilitating the workshop. As the Product Owner, he’s the natural choice. He’s the one who brought the project to life, connected the team with the shelter, and organized the experiment. Kim offers to support him. She has conducted user interviews before and feels comfortable talking to people about their work, asking questions, and trying to understand their experiences.
The plan for the day is straightforward. They start with a big picture Event Storming session to get an overview of the entire shelter domain. In the afternoon, they zoom in on Animal Intake. Leon thinks this is a good way to get everyone familiar with the method and the domain before exploring the first specific area in detail.
Sarah arrives at the company office. She knows the shelter’s daily operations inside out, but she hasn’t worked with this particular group before. She’s curious to see what they come up with.
The group enters the meeting room. There are no chairs around the table. In fact, there is hardly a table left in the room. The furniture is pushed against the walls, leaving plenty of space in front of the large whiteboard.
One of the basic rules of Event Storming: everyone stays on their feet. Sitting down makes it all too easy to slip into passive meeting mode. And once one person sits, others tend to follow.
Leon looks at the large, empty wall. He has prepared a short introduction, but he doesn’t want to spend too much time explaining a method nobody has experienced yet. They need to get started.
He looks around the room.
Leon picks up an orange sticky note and a marker.
That’s it. No elaborate explanation of colors, symbols, or modeling conventions. Just one simple idea: write down things that happened.
Leon has read about plenty of other concepts, too. Commands, actors, policies, aggregates, and all sorts of things that can be introduced during an Event Storming or Modeling session. But one piece of advice from the introductions he read sticks with him: don’t introduce concepts before the group needs them.
For now, orange sticky notes are enough.
The first few minutes are a little awkward.
Everyone looks at the wall, then at the sticky notes, then at each other. It isn’t that they have nothing to say. They’re simply not used to working this way. Usually, someone prepares a document or a diagram before a meeting. Here, they’re supposed to put their thoughts on the wall without knowing where they’ll end up.
Leon decides to make the first move.
He writes Animal Arrived At Shelter on an orange sticky note and puts it on the wall. Then he adds another one: Medical Treatment Done.
Chris follows. He writes down Microchip Scanned and adds it to the growing collection.
Kim and Mina start writing, too. They remember several things from Caramelo’s story and try to translate them into events. Sarah watches for a moment, apparently waiting to see what the team is doing. Then she picks up a marker herself and joins in.
Nobody is particularly concerned about the exact wording. Some notes describe broad activities, others are more specific. A few things appear twice. That’s perfectly fine.
After about fifteen minutes, the wall is covered with orange sticky notes. There’s no order to them, and nobody has tried to create one. But there’s already enough material to start a conversation.
Leon steps back and looks at the wall.

title: 9  Discovering the Big Picture
text: “Okay, that’s a great start. Now let’s see if we can put some order into this.”

title: 9  Discovering the Big Picture
text:
9.2 Finding the flow
The next step is to arrange the events from left to right, creating an imaginary timeline.
What happens first? What happens next? Which events belong before or after others?
It sounds simple enough, but as soon as they start moving the stickies around, discussions emerge.
Some events are easy to place. An animal has to arrive before it can be examined. That much is obvious. Other notes are less clear. Does something happen immediately after arrival, or can it happen later? Are two notes describing separate activities or different aspects of the same situation?
Kim is particularly interested in these discussions.
At first, she expects Event Storming to be a rather technical modeling exercise. But as she listens to Sarah explaining the reasons behind certain activities, she recognizes something familiar.
This isn’t so different from a user interview.
She’s used to asking people how they work, what happens when they encounter a particular situation, and what they do next. The difference is that now everyone can see the answers taking shape on the wall.
Instead of keeping her thoughts to herself, Kim starts asking more specific questions.


“Sarah, when an animal arrives, what do you usually do first? Is there something that happens for every animal, regardless of its condition?”


Sarah explains the initial steps. The others listen, occasionally adding a note or moving something that’s already on the wall.
Kim is getting into it.


“So, does that happen before the medical examination? Or is it part of the examination itself?”


Sarah explains that they scan the microchip as soon as an animal arrives.
Mina looks at the notes on the wall.


“Wait a minute. I thought the microchip was scanned during the medical check.”


Sarah clarifies that scanning the chip is part of the intake process. It doesn’t require a veterinarian. They want to identify the animal as early as possible, ideally finding out whether it has an owner who can be contacted.
Mina looks at Chris’s sticky note.


“Then this one belongs much earlier in the timeline.”


She moves Microchip Scanned towards the beginning.
It’s a small correction, but it changes how the team understands the process.
When they read Caramelo’s story, the microchip is scanned during the medical assessment. They simply assume that’s how things work. It seems reasonable enough. After all, checking a microchip sounds like something a veterinarian would do.
But Caramelo’s story isn’t a description of the shelter’s actual operations. It’s an introduction to the domain, and the team is now discovering that some of the details they take for granted don’t match reality.
Nobody deliberately makes a wrong decision. They’ve filled a gap in their understanding with an assumption they haven’t even noticed making.
Now the assumption is visible, and Sarah corrects it.
The team continues arranging the notes.

title: 9  Discovering the Big Picture
section: 9.3 When the wall starts talking back
text:
9.3 When the wall starts talking back
The conversation becomes more animated as the timeline develops.
Kim is now asking questions almost continuously. Chris contributes observations and occasionally suggests another event. Mina, who often keeps herself a little more in the background during group discussions, is increasingly involved.
Sarah is no longer simply answering questions. She’s pointing at notes, correcting the sequence, and adding things the team hasn’t thought of.
At one point, she explains what happens when the microchip scan identifies a registered owner.
That opens up an entirely new branch of the story.
Until now, the team has mostly been thinking about the animal’s journey through the shelter. But finding an owner introduces another process that can unfold alongside the animal’s care.
They start asking questions.
What happens when the registry returns an owner? How do they contact that person? What if the contact details are outdated? What if nobody answers?
The conversation quickly becomes more detailed than the team anticipates.
Chris is particularly interested in understanding how long they keep trying to reach the owner. There are several possibilities, and each seems to lead to another question.
Leon listens for a while. He doesn’t want to interrupt a useful discussion, but he also knows they’re supposed to be creating a big picture of the shelter domain, not solving every operational detail of Animal Intake right now.
He looks at the wall, then picks up a pink sticky note.
He turns it by forty-five degrees and writes a short question on it.


“Let’s park this one for a moment. I’ve read about a useful technique for exactly this situation. These are called Hot Spots. We use them to mark questions or topics that need further clarification.”


He places the pink note next to the branch they’ve just discovered.


“We don’t have to resolve everything right now. Let’s keep the question visible, continue with the bigger picture, and come back to it when we zoom into Animal Intake this afternoon.”


The group accepts the idea immediately.
They’ve encountered something they can’t answer yet, but there’s no need to lose track of it or spend the next twenty minutes trying to resolve it.
The Hot Spot gives the question a place on the wall without forcing them to answer it immediately.
As the workshop continues, more questions appear. Some are about missing information. Others highlight things that seem problematic or potentially inefficient in the process. The pink notes begin to accumulate around the orange ones.
Leon did not introduce a legend of every possible type of sticky note at the beginning. Whenever the group encounters a situation that calls for another concept, he introduces it.
The legend on the wall grows with the workshop.
And so does the team’s understanding of the shelter.

title: 9  Discovering the Big Picture
text:
9.4 The room comes alive
I have participated in many Event Storming sessions, and there’s a moment that I particularly enjoy.
It doesn’t happen at a predictable time. Sometimes it takes half an hour, sometimes longer. But at some point, the group becomes fully engaged.
People stop worrying about whether they’re doing the exercise correctly. They start discussing the actual business. Someone notices a missing step. Another person challenges an assumption. Sticky notes are moved around, questions are asked, and new connections emerge.
At this point, you can feel the energy in the room. It’s almost magical.
That’s what’s happening here.
Kim has found her rhythm. She’s asking questions that help Sarah explain the shelter’s work in more detail. Mina is actively contributing, too. She started the morning a little reserved, but the more they talk about the animals and what happens to them, the more interested she becomes.
She’s not just thinking about a software interface or a technical implementation. She genuinely wants to understand what happens to the animals.
Chris brings his usual enthusiasm into the conversation. Every new discovery seems to give him another idea or question. Occasionally, Leon has to bring the discussion back to the bigger picture, but Chris doesn’t seem to take that personally.
Sarah, too, is becoming more involved. She came prepared to explain how the shelter works. Now she’s collaborating with the team to build a picture of it.
The wall is no longer just a collection of sticky notes. It’s becoming a shared story.
And the team is beginning to see how much they didn’t know.

title: 9  Discovering the Big Picture
text:
9.5 Walking the story
After three hours, Leon decides it’s time to close the session.
There are still plenty of questions, and the wall is far from complete. But they’ve made good progress. They’ve explored the broad landscape of the shelter, discovered several branches in the process, and collected a number of questions for later clarification.
Leon suggests one final exercise.


“Before we stop, I’d like someone to walk us through the story we’ve created. Start at the beginning and follow the events on the wall, one by one. Tell us what happens, as if you’re explaining the shelter’s work to someone who has never seen it before.”


He looks around the room.


“Mina, would you like to give it a try?”


Mina looks a little surprised, but nods.
She steps towards the wall and begins at the left-hand side.


“Okay. So, an animal arrives at the shelter. The first thing they do is scan the microchip to see whether the animal can be identified. If they find a registered owner, they try to contact that person…”


She continues along the timeline, explaining the events and following the branches the team created.
Every now and then, she stops to check whether she understands something correctly. Sarah confirms some details and clarifies others.
Then Mina pauses at the alternative Intake branch.


“Wait. What happens to the animal while you’re trying to contact the owner?”


She looks at Sarah.
The question hasn’t been answered during the earlier discussion. They’ve focused on what happens when an owner can be identified, but they haven’t really explored what happens to the animal in parallel.
Leon picks up another pink sticky note.
Another Hot Spot.
The group briefly discusses the question, but decides to leave it for the afternoon. They don’t need to resolve every detail now. The important thing is that they’ve noticed the gap.
Mina continues.
There are a few more interruptions, a couple of corrections, and another question that ends up on the wall. That’s exactly what Leon hoped will happen.
When she finally reaches the end of the story, they step back and look at the result.
It isn’t a complete description of everything that happens in the shelter. Not even close.
But it’s a surprisingly coherent picture of a domain that most of them knew almost nothing about just a few hours earlier.

title: 9  Discovering the Big Picture
text:
9.6 Three hours well spent
Sarah looks at the wall for a moment.
She knows there are countless other things they can discuss. The shelter’s work is full of exceptions, special situations, and details that the team hasn’t even touched yet.
Still, she’s impressed.
The team managed to capture a good overview of the shelter’s operations in just three hours. More importantly, the questions they’ve asked show her that they’re genuinely interested in understanding how things work.
She has enjoyed the session.
The team, too, seems energized. They started the morning with some orange sticky notes and a little uncertainty about what to do with them. Now they have a wall full of events, several branches, and a growing collection of Hot Spots.
Leon is pleased. He was a little unsure how the workshop will unfold at first, but the format turns out to be much more natural than he expected. He didn’t need to explain a complicated method or had to control every conversation. His job was mostly to keep an eye on the bigger picture and help the group move forward.
Kim is still thinking about how familiar the whole experience feels. She expected to contribute through her designs and user journey expertise. Instead, she finds herself asking questions and helping Sarah tell the story. It feels surprisingly close to user research, only with everyone involved in making sense of the answers.
Mina is happy, too. She discovered that she can contribute much more than she initially thought. And the subject matter makes a difference. She genuinely cares about what happens to the animals.
Chris is already looking forward to exploring what they can do with all this information.
Sarah thanks the team and says she’s looking forward to the afternoon. There’s still a lot to discuss, but the morning was both fun and productive.
They agree to meet again after lunch.
After three hours on their feet, the team leaves the room for a well-deserved break. They enjoy lunch together, chatting about all sorts of things. But sooner or later, the conversation finds its way back to the workshop.
They talk about the microchip discovery, the different branches of the story, and the questions they’ve parked for later.
Three hours earlier, none of them knew quite what to expect.
Now they’re looking forward to doing it again.
Only this time, they’ll zoom in.




Brandolini, Alberto. 2021. Introducing EventStorming. leanpup.com.

title: 10  From Events To Screens
text:
10.1 How do you make toast?
When the team returns from lunch, the wall still looks the same as they left it. The orange event notes stretch across it, with a few pink Hot Spots interrupting the timeline. Three hours of discussion have produced a somewhat coherent picture of the shelter’s work. At least, that’s how it feels.
Leon waits until everyone has settled around the wall. Well, settled might be the wrong word. Nobody is sitting. The chairs and tables are still pushed against the walls, and the team is getting used to spending the day on its feet.
He pauses and looks at Sarah.
Leon explains that they want to map the user journey and the screens that support it. They will start with Animal Intake, their focus for the afternoon, rather than trying to design the entire application.
Kim steps closer to the wall. She has been listening, but now she seems to be in her element.
She picks up a broad marker and holds it up.
Mina smiles. She knows exactly how easily a discussion about a button can consume half an hour.
But before they start sketching screens for the shelter, Kim suggests a small exercise.
Chris looks at her.
There is a brief silence, followed by the sound of markers moving across paper.
Leon draws a sequence of boxes connected by arrows. Get bread. Put bread in toaster. Toast bread. Take toast out. Add butter. Chris starts with a picture of a toaster and bread, then adds a hand reaching for the lever. Mina draws a neat sequence, including a step for choosing the desired browning level. Kim’s sketch includes a person, a toaster, a plate, and a small decision about whether the bread is already toasted enough.
Sarah is just as busy with her marker. Her drawing starts with a slice of bread and a toaster, but she adds a few steps the others haven’t thought about. She draws a cupboard where she gets the bread, then a plate, and finally a jar of jam. Apparently, toast at Sarah’s place involves a little more than butter.
When they put the sheets next to each other, the differences are immediately visible.
Chris laughs and points at Mina’s sketch.
Kim looks at the five sketches side by side. They all understand what making toast means. They probably make toast regularly. Yet they have drawn different processes, included different steps, and made different assumptions about what matters.
Leon looks back at the wall of orange notes.
The exercise takes barely ten minutes, but it changes the atmosphere. The team has a shared reference for the next step, and nobody feels the need to produce a beautiful design. In fact, the rougher the sketches, the easier it is to talk about them.
Kim takes a large sheet of paper and draws a rough rectangle. She adds a few larger areas inside it, using the broad marker to make the structure visible.

title: 10  From Events To Screens
text:
“Let’s try something first. Everyone gets a sheet of paper. Draw how to make toast. Don’t discuss it with anyone. Just draw the steps as you imagine them.”





“Toast? As in bread and toaster?”




“Exactly. Nothing complicated. You have five minutes.”








“Wait. Leon, you don’t even have a plate.”




“I didn’t think the plate was part of making toast.”




“But where do you put it after taking it out of the toaster?”




“In my hand, presumably.”





“And she has a browning-level decision. I just push the lever down and hope for the best.”





“That’s the point. We all heard the same task, but we didn’t imagine exactly the same thing. Some things were obvious to one person and not to another. And we only noticed because we put the sketches next to each other.”





“So perhaps we shouldn’t assume that we all imagine the same thing when we say Animal Intake.”




“Exactly. And that’s why I wanted everyone to sketch first. We can compare what we have and talk about the differences. We don’t need to agree on a design before we’ve understood what people actually need.”

title: 10  From Events To Screens
text:
10.2 Sketching the first screens


“This is all we’re after. A sketch that helps us talk. We can add details later.”


They turn to the Animal Intake timeline. The orange events are still arranged in the order they established in the morning. Now they begin to think about the screens a shelter employee might use along the way.
The first idea is an Occupancy Board. It gives staff an overview of the animals currently in the shelter and helps them see where things stand. Kim draws a broad screen with several distinct areas. Chris suggests making the animals easy to distinguish at a glance. Mina asks what information someone needs when looking at the board during a busy day. Sarah contributes examples from the shelter’s daily routines, explaining what staff usually want to know when checking the current situation.
They do not try to settle every detail. The purpose is to make the screen tangible enough that they can discuss it.
Next comes the Animal Registration Form. Kim sketches a rough form with a few obvious sections. Leon looks at the orange notes around the arrival and registration events and asks which parts of the process the form should support. Sarah helps them distinguish information that staff collect when an animal arrives from information they may only learn later.
The sketches begin to accumulate. Each large white sheet represents a screen or a meaningful part of the user journey. The team places them above the corresponding events on the timeline, keeping the sequence they established in the morning.
As the discussion progresses, the wall starts to change. It is no longer just a timeline of things that happen. There are now screens above it, connected to the events they help bring about.
Kim steps back to look at the growing arrangement.


“I think we’re getting somewhere. But the screens are still just boxes. We need to understand what information each one displays and what information people enter.”


Leon nods. That’s the next step. For every screen, they want to identify the properties that need to be visible. And where the user enters information, they also want to capture the data collected by the interface.
They introduce two more colors of sticky notes. Green for the properties displayed on a screen, blue for the data collected through the UI. These go below the corresponding screen, with the orange events remaining underneath. The arrangement gives them a vertical slice: the screen, the information it displays or collects, and the event associated with it.

title: 10  From Events To Screens
text:
10.3 What sits behind a screen
At first, this sounds straightforward. They have the screens. They know the events. Surely, filling in the information between them is mostly a matter of listing fields.
But the first few questions already suggest otherwise.
The first screen they tackle in more detail is the Occupancy Board.
At a glance, it seems simple enough. A board showing the animals currently staying at the shelter, perhaps grouped by their location. The team starts listing the information someone might need when looking at it: the animal’s name, species, perhaps a photo, its current location, and some indication of its status.
Chris suggests that they could make the board interactive. A staff member could select an animal and move it to another kennel. Mina immediately asks what happens if the destination kennel is already occupied.
That question sends them back to Sarah.
Sarah explains that the shelter has different kinds of accommodation for different animals. You cannot simply put any animal into any available space. The team starts asking how staff know which kennels are suitable, how they know whether a kennel is available, and how they keep track of animals that are expected to move out.
They add more green sticky notes beneath the Occupancy Board. But the more information they list, the less the screen looks like a self-contained feature.
Someone asks whether the board should also show kennels that are currently occupied but expected to become available soon. That leads to another question: how does the shelter know when a kennel will become free? Is there a planned departure date? What happens when an animal is moved to foster care? And who is responsible for updating the information?
The discussion moves away from the screen itself. They are no longer talking only about what a user should see. They are trying to understand how the shelter manages its accommodation.
Leon looks at the growing collection of notes beneath the sketch. The Occupancy Board still looks like one screen, but the information behind it seems to require quite a bit more than a handful of fields.


“Hang on. I thought we were designing an overview screen. Now we’re discussing how the shelter manages its kennels.”




“Because the screen needs that information. We can’t decide what to show without understanding where it comes from.”


Mina studies the notes.


“And we can’t make the board useful if the information isn’t maintained somewhere. If a kennel becomes available, someone needs to record that. If an animal is expected to leave next week, we need to know that too.”


Chris is already thinking about possible interactions.


“We could have a separate kennel management screen. Maybe a calendar view for reservations, and then …”


Leon raises a hand, smiling.


“Let’s not design the whole application just yet. First, let’s understand what Sarah and the shelter staff actually need.”


Sarah continues explaining how they work today. Some of the information is recorded in a spreadsheet on a shared drive, some is kept in people’s heads, and some depends on staff knowing the current situation. The team realizes that the Occupancy Board is only the visible part of a much larger capability.
They add a few more notes and mark questions they cannot answer yet. The original sketch has not become useless. Quite the opposite. It has helped them discover what they need to understand before they can design it properly.
And this is where the afternoon starts to feel different from the morning.

title: 10  From Events To Screens
text:
10.4 The iceberg beneath the board
During the Big Picture Event Storming, the team moved quickly. Events gave them a way to explore a broad domain without having to understand every detail. They could follow the story, add what happened, and keep moving. Three hours later, they had a timeline that felt complete.
Now they are looking at one screen and discovering how much sits behind it.
The Occupancy Board is a good example because nobody questioned its existence in the morning. Everyone could imagine a board showing the animals in the shelter. It sounded so obvious that there was no reason to stop and investigate it.
But the moment they ask what information it needs, the picture changes. Kennels have types and capacities. They can be occupied, become available, or be reserved for an animal expected to arrive. Animals move between locations, and staff need to know not only where an animal is now but where it might be next week.
What looked like a screen is turning into a domain of its own: shelter accommodation management.
The team has not designed that module, and they certainly have not agreed on all its rules. They have simply discovered that the apparently simple Occupancy Board depends on a much larger understanding of how the shelter manages its space.
Leon looks at the wall again. The morning’s timeline is still there, but now the space above it is filling with screens and the space below those screens with information. The model is getting wider and deeper at the same time.
The iceberg is becoming visible. And they have only started with one screen.
He slowly starts to realize what Event Modeling is about, and how it might indeed be the missing ingredient for Agentic Engineering.

title: 11  After The Storm
text:
11.1 Reporting back to Claire
Leon sits at his desk, looking at the photos1 from yesterday’s workshop. The wall is crowded with events, questions, sketches, and small clusters of notes. Some parts look orderly. Others are a mess. He zooms in on a section, reads a note, then zooms out again.
He is trying to put his thoughts into a form that makes sense. Not a workshop report. Claire doesn’t need a list of everything the team did during the day. She wants to know whether the experiment is moving in the right direction, and Leon wants to understand that himself.
The morning started slowly. Nobody in the team has done Event Storming together before, and the first few minutes felt a little awkward. But once the events began to accumulate, people started connecting things. Questions lead to more questions. Sarah, the shelter director, became part of the discovery rather than someone who simply answers what the team asks.
That is one of the things Leon keeps thinking about. The team didn’t just collect information from Sarah. They explored the domain with her. And sometimes they discovered that what they think they know is wrong. The microchip is a good example. Caramelo’s story gave them the impression that the chip is checked during the medical examination. Sarah explained that they scan it immediately when an animal arrives. A small correction, perhaps, but it changes the sequence the team had in mind.
In the afternoon, Kim took the group from the events to screens and user journeys. Leon expected the change of perspective to be useful, but he didn’t expect it to reveal another part of the domain they haven’t considered. The Occupancy Board did exactly that. What initially looked like a screen for displaying animals turned into a discussion about kennels, animal locations, availability, and the information shelter staff need to decide where an animal can stay.
The day leaves Leon with a strange combination of excitement and uncertainty. They made more progress than he expected, but the more they discovered, the more he saw how much they still don’t know.
He closes the photos and heads to Claire’s office.
Claire looks up when he enters.
Leon smiles.
Leon takes a seat. He has a few points in mind, but he doesn’t want to turn the conversation into a presentation.
Leon thinks for a moment.
Claire leans back.
He pauses, searching for the right words.
Claire nods, but doesn’t immediately respond.

title: 11  After The Storm
text:
“So, how was the storm?”





“Better than I expected. And more interesting than I expected, too.”




“That’s a promising start. What makes you say that?”





“The engagement, mainly. I wasn’t sure how the team would react. None of us has worked this way together before. The first part was a little slow, but once we got going, everyone contributed. And Sarah was not just answering questions. She started exploring the process with us.”




“What is different about that compared with your usual requirements workshops?”





“Usually, we arrive with a pretty good idea of what we want to ask. We collect the answers, Kim documents the requirements, and then we work out what needs to be built. Yesterday, we didn’t really know what we are looking for yet. We started with a simple question about what happens when an animal arrives, and the next question often came from something someone else noticed.”




“And that works?”




“Surprisingly well. We uncovered things we didn’t know, and we didn’t have to pretend that we have an answer. We marked the questions and kept going. Otherwise, we could have spent half the morning discussing one detail.”




“You mean the Hot Spots?”




“Exactly. It gave us a way to keep track of the open questions without losing the bigger picture.”





“You sound impressed by the technique. But what about the result? Do you understand the animal intake process better now?”




“Definitely. We have a much better overview than I expected after just one morning. And we have it together. That’s probably the part that surprises me most.”




“Together?”




“Yes. Sarah knows the shelter’s work, of course. But she doesn’t necessarily think about it in the same way we do. And we don’t all look at it from the same angle either. Kim noticed things about the user journey. Mina spoted gaps in the process. Chris asked questions about what happens behind the scenes. I think we got a more complete picture because everyone was looking at the same thing.”





“I also noticed that people became more involved as the board grew. Mina, for example. She was quite reserved at the beginning, but later she actively joined the discussion. During the final walkthrough, she spoted a question we haven’t addressed. It feels like the model gives everyone something concrete to react to.”

title: 11  After The Storm
text:
11.2 One screen, many assumptions


“And the afternoon?”




“That was interesting in a different way. Kim took us through the user journey using sketches. I think she enjoyed that part.”




“I can imagine.”




“She has a good eye for how people use a system. But we also discovered that we don’t always imagine the same interaction when we look at a screen.”




“So even a simple screen can mean different things to different people.”




“Apparently. And the Occupancy Board took us somewhere we didn’t expect. We started talking about where animals stay, how kennels are assigned, and what the staff need to know before they can make a decision. It opened up another part of the domain.”




“Does that mean you missed something in the morning?”




“I wouldn’t say we missed it. We simply didn’t see it until we looked at the process from the perspective of the screens. The events give us one view. The user journey gives us another.”


Claire looks at him for a moment.

title: 11  After The Storm
text:
11.3 From workshop to working software


“That sounds useful. But I want to be careful here. A productive workshop is not necessarily a better way of building software. What do you think changes when you move from this result to implementation?”


Leon expected the question. It is also the question he has been asking himself since the workshop.


“I don’t know yet. We have a better understanding of the domain, and I think that gives us a better starting point for the specification. But we haven’t built anything. We haven’t worked with an agent on the basis of this model. So I can’t tell you whether it will make implementation more reliable.”




“Good. I would be worried if you could already tell me that.”


Leon laughs.


“I know. But I do see a connection. If we want AI agents to implement software, we need to give them more than a collection of tickets and a few screens. Yesterday gave me the feeling that we can make our understanding more explicit before we ask an agent to do anything.”




“And the model is supposed to become the specification?”




“That’s the idea. At least, that’s what I want to explore. But right now, we have a board full of discoveries. We need to work out how to turn that into something we can actually use.”


Claire glances at the notes on her desk.


“What do you think the team needs next?”


Leon shifts in his chair. This is the part he has been preparing for.

title: 11  After The Storm
text:
11.4 Asking for help


“I think we need some help getting started with Event Modeling in prooph board.”




“Why? Didn’t you just spend a day modeling the process?”




“We explored it together, yes. But we haven’t developed an Event Model before. I don’t want us to spend the next week figuring out the tool and the conventions by trial and error. We need a first step that builds on what we already discovered.”




“And who do you have in mind?”




“Alex.”


Claire raises her eyebrows slightly.


“The prooph board Alex?”




“That’s the one. We’ve been in touch for a while. He offered us additional free seats if we make Shelter Flow open source. I think this is a good opportunity to ask him for a hands-on session.”




“What kind of session?”


Leon opens his laptop and turns it slightly towards Claire. He has a few notes on the screen. They are not a detailed agenda, but enough to show that he has thought about the proposal.


“A remote working session, half a day. We start with the results from yesterday, not with a generic example. Alex guides us step by step through developing what we discovered into an Event Model in prooph board. The team learns by doing, using Shelter Flow itself.”


Claire reads the notes.


“What do you expect to have at the end?”




“A first part of our model, and a better understanding of how to continue. I don’t expect Alex to model the whole product for us. He can show us how to approach it, explain the decisions behind the modeling, and help us avoid some obvious mistakes. The domain decisions remain ours. Sarah and the team know the shelter’s work. Alex can help us express what we discovered in the model.”




“And after the session?”




“We continue ourselves. I would like the team to become comfortable enough with the approach that we can develop the model as we learn more about the product.”


Claire looks back at the notes.


“Half a day is reasonable. But I don’t want this to become another training session where everyone leaves with a nice collection of slides and then goes back to working as before.”




“Neither do I. That’s why I want to work on our own model. We should have something useful at the end, not just a theoretical understanding of the tool.”




“Then make sure Alex understands that. And make sure the team doesn’t treat his way of doing things as a recipe they have to follow. I want them to understand why they make modeling decisions, not just which buttons to click.”




“Agreed. I’ll ask him to help us shape the session around the workshop results. I have only sketched the agenda so far.”


Claire closes the laptop and looks at Leon.


“All right. Go ahead and arrange it. Keep it within the experiment’s budget, of course. And I want to hear what the team takes away from it, not just whether they like the tool.”




“Fair enough.”


Leon stands up. He feels a little more confident than when he entered the office. The workshop doesn’t prove that their new approach works, but it gives him something concrete to build on. And now they have a next step.

title: 11  After The Storm
text:
11.5 Time to start designing
Back at his desk, he opens his messages and finds Alex’s conversation. He starts typing, briefly considers how much context to include, then decides that the workshop results are the best place to begin.
He proposes a half-day remote working session with the team. They want to take what they have discovered about animal intake and develop it into their first Event Model. He asks Alex to help them shape the agenda and guide them through the process, using their own findings rather than a prepared example.
Leon sends the message and looks once more at the workshop photos.
The storm has passed. It is time to start designing.
